title: Analyzing categorical data: Visual Guide
outline: Title: Analyzing categorical data: Visual Guide

1. Table You Already Know | a confusion matrix of 200 messages with its margins and grand total, and a slider over the share that really is spam, printing the row reading (recall) beside the column reading (precision) | the bridge from what you already know: a confusion matrix IS a two-way table, and the same four counts give different percentages depending on which total you divide by — the filter never changes, only the margins do

2. One Variable, Counted | three category counts on sliders driving a bar chart and a frequency table of counts, relative frequencies and percentages, plus a button that reorders the categories | a categorical variable's values are labels, so counting and dividing by the total are the only operations available; relative frequency is count over total and the percentages sum to 100% for any sample size, which is what licenses a pie chart

3. Margins And Grand Total | a 2x2 two-way table of athletes and exam results built cell by cell on four sliders, with live row totals, column totals and the grand total reached three ways | the margins are sums of cells and the grand total is the sum of all four cells, reachable identically down the rows or across the columns; margins are counts so they add to the grand total, never to 100, and each one is the denominator of a conditional proportion

4. Three Ways To Divide | one frozen 100-student table under four denominators — counts, joint percent, row percent, column percent — with any cell tappable to show all of its readings at once | joint, marginal and conditional are the same table under three denominators: 15/100 = 15% of everyone, 15/20 = 75% of the athletes, 15/55 = 27% of those who passed, and a conditional distribution by row reports percentages within each row

5. Spotting Association | 200 people split into two groups by one slider and separated in yes-rate by another, drawn as two conditional distributions with raw counts, expected counts and a computed verdict | conditional distributions nearly the same across the groups suggests little or no association, and raw counts must not be compared across groups of different sizes — at some settings the counts even point the opposite way to the rates
